pedagogy.summary: Children solve elapsed-time word problems in both directions — find the END time given a start and a duration, and find the DURATION between two times — using a blank number line. They count on in convenient jumps (to the next o'clock, whole hours, then minutes). The persistent errors are treating time as base-10 (adding minutes past 60 without rolling the hour), column subtraction that fails across the hour boundary, and counting in the wrong direction.
bestPractices: Use a blank number line for both problem types; count on in jumps (next o'clock, whole hours, minutes)
Decide the direction first: adding a duration forwards vs finding the gap between two times
Bridge the o'clock rather than subtracting in columns
Represent the story on the line before calculating (start, jumps, end)
Check the answer against a clock face
keyRepresentations: Blank number line with labelled jumps
The 'bridge to the next o'clock' jump
commonMisconceptions: Adds the duration to the minutes only, ignoring the hour roll-over past 60 (2:15 + 47 -> '2:62')
Column subtraction of the two times, failing across the hour boundary
Counts in the wrong direction (subtracts a duration instead of adding, or vice versa)
Overshoots or undershoots the o'clock bridge (base-10 slip)

learn.summary: Children solve elapsed-time word problems in both directions — finding the END time from a start and a duration, and finding the DURATION between two times — using a blank number line and counting on in convenient jumps (to the next o'clock, then whole hours, then minutes). The core teaching move is showing that the SAME number line solves both 'when does it end?' and 'how long is it?', so elapsed time becomes one count-on method rather than two mysterious sums. Persistent errors to target: treating time as base-10 by writing minutes past 60 without rolling the hour over (2:15 + 47 -> '2:62'), column subtraction that fails across the hour boundary, and counting in the wrong direction.

activities.title: Count on along a number line to find the end time
feedback: If a learner writes an end time with 60 or more minutes (e.g. '2:62' or '3:75'), ask: 'Can a time have 62 minutes? What happens at 60?' Then bridge to the next o'clock first (2:15 -> 3:00) and add the rest.
If the first jump overshoots or undershoots the o'clock, ask 'How many minutes from 2:15 to the next whole hour?' before adding the remaining minutes.
Confirm success by checking: 3:40 + 35 = jump +20 to 4:00 then +15 = 4:15, with the hour correctly rolled over.
activities.rationale: A blank number line lets children bridge to the next o'clock rather than add minutes past 60, directly addressing the base-10 slip. Research documents that children apply base-10 whole-number reasoning to time and struggle to coordinate its base-60 groupings, which produces minutes-past-60 errors; a published scheme of learning uses the blank number line with jumps to whole hours and minutes for exactly this purpose.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y4 Time (Step 3) documents using a blank number line to find durations and start/end times (e.g. jumps of +1 hour and +10 minutes), and warns that children may attempt to calculate durations using column subtraction, leading to inaccuracies when hours are crossed.

Children apply base-10 whole-number reasoning to time and cannot easily coordinate its base-60 groupings, explaining minutes-past-60 errors (2:15 + 47 -> '2:62') and column-subtraction failures across the hour boundary.
learnerActions: Read a word problem such as: 'A film starts at 2:15 and lasts 47 minutes — when does it end?'
Draw a blank number line and mark the start time (2:15).
Make a first jump that bridges to the next o'clock: +45 minutes to reach 3:00.
Make a second jump with the remaining minutes: +2 to reach 3:02; label each jump and read off the end time.
Repeat with a harder bridge: 'Swimming starts at 3:40 and lasts 35 minutes — when does it finish?' Jump +20 to 4:00, then +15 to reach 4:15.
Check the end time on a clock face.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding a duration means counting FORWARD from the start; bridging to the next o'clock first makes the hour roll over correctly, so you never write an impossible time like 2:62 or 3:75.

activities.title: Fill the gap to find a duration
feedback: If a learner sets out 10:05 minus 9:20 in columns and borrows in base-10, show that this fails across the hour boundary; model counting on in jumps to the o'clock then the minutes instead.
If a learner adds 9:20 and 10:05 together, ask 'Are you finding how LONG it is or adding two moments? Which jumps fill the gap?'
Reinforce that the two jumps (+40 then +5) sum to the answer the same way the end-time jumps did.
activities.rationale: Modelling a duration as a filled gap counteracts the column-subtraction error that fails across the hour boundary, which a published scheme of learning explicitly warns about, and which research links to base-10 reasoning applied to base-60 time.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y4 Time (Step 3) documents using a blank number line to find durations and start/end times (e.g. jumps of +1 hour and +10 minutes), and warns that children may attempt to calculate durations using column subtraction, leading to inaccuracies when hours are crossed.

Children apply base-10 whole-number reasoning to time and cannot easily coordinate its base-60 groupings, explaining minutes-past-60 errors (2:15 + 47 -> '2:62') and column-subtraction failures across the hour boundary.
learnerActions: Read a problem such as: 'How many minutes are there between 9:20 and 10:05?'
On a blank number line, mark both times (9:20 and 10:05).
Jump from the earlier time to the next o'clock: +40 minutes to reach 10:00.
Jump the remaining minutes: +5 to reach 10:05.
Add the jumps together (40 + 5) to get the total duration of 45 minutes.
Check against a clock face, and explain why adding 9:20 and 10:05 together would be nonsense.
activities.intendedInsight: Finding a duration means filling the GAP between two times with jumps and summing them — not subtracting in columns and not adding the two clock times together. Bridging the o'clock keeps the base-60 boundary correct.

activities.title: Decide the direction before you jump
feedback: If a learner counts backward on a 'find the end' problem, or forward on a 'find the start', pause and re-ask: 'Is the unknown an end time, a start time, or how long it lasted? Which way do the jumps go?'
If a learner adds 9:20 and 10:05 when asked for a gap, restate that a gap is filled with jumps between the two times, never a sum of the clock readings.
Praise correct identification of the unknown and direction before any arithmetic begins.
activities.rationale: Explicitly rehearsing whether the unknown is an end time, start time, or duration addresses the directional/performance error where children subtract a duration that should be added, or add two clock times. Using the one number line for all three cases shows elapsed time as a single jump-counting method, counting forward or backward and bridging the o'clock.
learnerActions: Before calculating any problem, state out loud whether the unknown is an END time (jump forward from the start by the duration), a START time (jump backward from the end by the duration) or a GAP (fill the space between two given times).
Solve a mixed set, e.g. 'A show ends at 10:05 and lasted 45 minutes — when did it START?' by counting BACKWARD: -5 to 10:00, then -40 to 9:20.
Compare a forward problem and a backward problem side by side, labelling which way the jumps go.
Say which number is unknown and which direction the jumps travel before marking the line.
activities.intendedInsight: Choosing the direction first — forward to find an end, backward to find a start, or filling the gap to find a duration — prevents counting the wrong way or adding two clock times together.

constraints: Pupils should already read and record time in seconds, minutes and hours and compare durations before tackling these word problems; if they write times with 60+ minutes, revisit how 60 minutes rolls the hour over before continuing.

Multiple-choice or fill-in-the-blank items about elapsed time can check whether answers are correct, but they do not show whether the child built the jumps or bridged the o'clock; pair them with a 'show your jumps' task so the method is visible.
A fixed worked-example diagram can illustrate the jumps but does not let the child build them in either direction; use it as a reference, not as the main practice.
A spoken or dialogue format can pose word problems and prompt reasoning, but still needs the child to actually draw and label jumps so the method is practised, not just discussed.

An interactive number line where jumps are dragged and a clock rolls over as each jump lands can make the hour roll-over visible in real time; this is one helpful presentation, not a requirement — the same learning can happen with pencil-and-paper number lines and a physical clock face.
Always state the known times explicitly (the start time for end-time problems, both times for duration problems, and the end time for start-time problems) so the direction of counting is unambiguous.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original source row rated a 3D interactive as adding nothing and a static image/conversation as unable to let the child build jumps. These catalog-style comparative claims have been softened into scoped notes about affordances and limits rather than universal pedagogical laws.

Arithmetic self-check: 2:15 + 47 min = +45 to 3:00 then +2 = 3:02 (correct); 3:40 + 35 = +20 to 4:00 then +15 = 4:15 (correct); 9:20 to 10:05 = +40 then +5 = 45 min (correct); backward 10:05 − 45 = −5 to 10:00 then −40 = 9:20 (correct). The erroneous learner outputs '2:62' and '3:75' are retained only as misconceptions to diagnose and correct, never as valid answers.
The original row listed a prerequisite reteach id for base-60/hour-crossing; that internal identifier has been dropped in favour of the plain-language prerequisite stated in constraints.

The 'decide the direction' activity targets a performance error (wrong-direction counting) that had no directly supporting source claim in the original row, so its sourceClaims is left empty; the number-line method itself is sourced on the first two activities.

probeDeeper: 'Show me your first jump — where did you land?' (o'clock bridge)
'Your answer says 2:62 — can a time have 62 minutes? What happens at 60?'
'Are you finding when it ENDS, or how LONG it is? Which way do the jumps go?'
'A show ends at 10:05 and lasted 45 minutes — when did it START?' (backward count-on)
assess.correctAnswer: For the film, counts on 2:15 to 3:00 (+45) then +2 = 3:02 (or +47 bridging correctly); for 9:20 to 10:05 counts +40 to 10:00, +5 = 45 minutes; for 3:40 + 35 bridges to 4:00 (+20), +15 = 4:15 — rolling the hour over rather than writing 3:75.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds the duration to the minutes only, ignoring the hour roll-over past 60 (2:15 + 47 -> '2:62')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the number line to bridge to the next o'clock first (2:15 -> 3:00), then add the rest; show that 60 minutes rolls the hour over.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes an end time with minutes of 60 or more; doesn't bridge to the next hour

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses column subtraction of the two times, failing across the hour boundary
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model counting on to fill the gap (jumps to the o'clock, then minutes); make the base-60 boundary explicit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 10:05 minus 9:20 in columns and borrows base-10, getting a wrong gap

errorPatterns.pattern: Counts in the wrong direction — subtracts a duration when it should be added on, or adds the two clock times together when finding a gap
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold: decide first whether the unknown is an end time (jump forward by the duration) or a gap (fill between the two times); rehearse choosing the direction before jumping.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On 'find the end' counts backwards; on 'find the gap' adds 9:20 and 10:05

responseLevels.gap: Adds minutes past 60 or subtracts in columns; counts the wrong direction; can't cross the hour.
responseLevels.full: Solves both elapsed-time directions on a number line, bridging the o'clock, rolling the hour over correctly, and choosing the right direction for the unknown.
responseLevels.partial: Solves within-hour problems and one direction reliably, but slips crossing the hour or on the reverse (find-start / find-duration) case.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set both problem types and WATCH: (1) 'A film starts at 2:15 and lasts 47 minutes — when does it end? Show me your jumps.' (2) 'How many minutes between 9:20 and 10:05?' (3) A crossing-the-hour end-time: 'Swimming starts at 3:40 and lasts 35 minutes — when does it finish?' Watch whether they count on with a number line (bridging the o'clock) or add minutes past 60, subtract in columns, or go the wrong direction.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The hour-crossing items catch the child who adds minutes past 60 (2:15 + 47 -> '2:62'; 3:40 + 35 -> '3:75') or subtracts in columns; a child bridging the o'clock on a number line rolls the hour correctly. Doing both directions catches counting the wrong way.
